description: Public health and healthtech professionals joining for the Astronaut Health Monitoring challenge. Looking for teammates in Python, AI, bioinformatics, or data visualization. Let's build something exciting!
summary:
HealthRADAR+ is a prototype that helps astronauts decide what to do about a health problem when Earth is too far away to help quickly. It uses synthetic data only.

An assistant called Orby watches simulated wearable, habitat and suit data and listens to a crew member describe a symptom in their own words. Orby is rule-based, not a trained AI model: it asks follow-up questions using transparent rules and never gives a diagnosis. Readings appear on an interactive 3D body, habitat and suit, and the rules, supplies and communication delay change across five mission profiles, from the ISS to the Mars surface. An augmented reality (AR) guide then overlays the exam steps on the crew member’s own body through a camera, with voice control.

The app compares findings with the crew member’s own baseline, then weighs medical supplies, communication delay and how fast the problem is getting worse. The crew records a decision, monitoring takes over, and the case is reassessed and closed.

It addresses the challenge by supporting care on long-duration missions with limited resources and communication delays. It is a prototype and has not been clinically validated.
details:
HealthRADAR+ follows one case from the first sign of trouble to follow-up, using the RADAR steps: Recognize, Assess, Decide, Act and Reassess.

  1. Recognize. Simulated wearable, habitat and suit streams are compared with each crew member’s own baseline. A crew member can also describe a symptom to Orby in free text, and Orby asks rule-based follow-up questions.
  2. Analyze. Seven practice exams (ultrasound, ECG, blood sample, eye exam, vital signs and others) run as 3D step-by-step guides. In the augmented reality (AR) guide, the camera finds the user’s shoulders, arms, face and hands and overlays the exam landmarks on their body, with voice control. The app then interprets the findings.
  3. Decide. The app weighs the findings, medical supplies, communication delay and how fast the problem is progressing. The crew records a decision.
  4. Act. Orby is told the decision, and the plan (treat, monitor, repeat an exam or evacuate) is carried out. Monitoring takes over and watches the triggers that were set.
  5. Reassess. If a trigger is met, or the repeat exam is due, the app prompts a reassessment. The crew then updates the decision or closes the case once the patient is better or worse.

Benefits and intended impact
It helps a crew act sooner and more consistently when ground support is delayed. Every answer shows the rule behind it, and nothing is a diagnosis. The aim is to show how decision support could reduce uncertainty on long missions, not to replace flight surgeons.

Tools and technology
Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single static page hosted on GitHub Pages. Three.js for the 3D body, habitat and suit; MediaPipe Pose for body tracking; and the browser’s camera and speech features for AR and voice. Playwright for automated testing. We used Claude (an AI assistant) to help write and test the code. 3D models are credited on the app’s Credits page.

Creativity
It joins monitoring, a camera-based AR exam, stock-aware decisions and follow-up into one case, instead of separate dashboards. The AR works on a laptop webcam with no headset.

What we considered
Safety and honesty (all data is synthetic, no diagnoses, not clinically validated), transparency of the rules, working with no special hardware, accessibility, and the limits of communication delay between mission types.
